0.title: Already and Not Yet
0.essay:
Every Christian lives in two times at once. The new age of God has already begun in Jesus Christ, and the old age of sin and death has not yet ended. Learning to live in that overlap is one of the keys to the whole Christian life.

Two ages and one great day

By the time of Jesus, many Jews thought of history in two parts: “this age” of sin, sickness and death, and “the age to come”, when God would pour out his Spirit, raise the dead and make “new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). Between them stood one great day, the day of the LORD. One age would end and the other begin, as cleanly as one day follows another.

Jesus used the same language (Matthew 12:32). But what he did was startling. He brought the age to come into the middle of this age. In his healings, his resurrection and the gift of the Spirit, the future arrived early. Yet the old age did not stop. So the two ages overlap until he returns.

Dawn while the night remains

Paul gives us a picture. “The night is far gone; the day is at hand” (Romans 13:12). Think of the hour before sunrise. The eastern sky is already light, and no one doubts the sun is coming. Yet the streets are still dark and the frost still lies on the ground. John says the same: “the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining” (1 John 2:8).

Two levels, one pattern

This overlap is true on two levels: of the world, where Christ reigns yet evil still fights, and of your own heart, where you are already a new creation yet still fight temptation and sin. These are one pattern, because the believer is a small piece of the new creation living in an old world. The study The Kingdom of God sets out the global side briefly in its unit Already and Not Yet: Living Between the Ages. This study goes further, and brings the pattern home.

The chapters

Two Ages in Scripture; The World Between the Ages; Already New; Not Yet Finished; Living in the Overlap; and When Not Yet Becomes Now.

For reflection

Where in your life do you most feel the “already”, and where the “not yet”? Have you ever been confused or discouraged because you expected one without the other?

1.title: Two Ages in Scripture
1.essay:
The idea of two overlapping ages is not a clever scheme laid on top of the Bible. It is woven through the New Testament, often in small phrases that are easy to read past.

The end of the ages has come

Writing to the church in Corinth, Paul says the Old Testament stories were written “for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). That is an astonishing thing to say to a small, quarrelsome congregation in a Greek port. The goal of all history has arrived in Christ, and these ordinary believers are living in it.

Yet in the same letter Paul says plainly that the end is still ahead, when Christ “delivers the kingdom to God the Father” (1 Corinthians 15:24). The end has come, and the end is coming. Paul does not feel this as a contradiction. It is simply the shape of the time he lives in.

Rescued from the present evil age

Paul opens Galatians by saying that Christ “gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age” (Galatians 1:4). Notice what he does not say. He does not say Christ has ended the present evil age. It is still here, and it is still evil. But Christians have been rescued out of it while it goes on. Their citizenship, their life and their future now belong to another age.

So Paul tells the Romans not to be “conformed to this world” (Romans 12:2), where “world” is literally “age”. The old age still presses on us. We belong to the new one.

Tasting the powers of the age to come

Hebrews describes Christian experience in a beautiful phrase. Believers have “tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come” (Hebrews 6:5). A taste is real. It is not an imitation of the meal. But it is not the whole meal either. Every time the gospel opens a hard heart, every answered prayer, every moment when the Spirit makes Christ sweet to you, you are tasting the future ahead of time.

Meanwhile Christ himself already reigns over both ages. God has seated him “far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come” (Ephesians 1:21). The King of the coming age is not waiting to take his throne. He has it now.

Between two appearings

Titus 2 puts the two ages side by side in one sentence. The grace of God has appeared, training us “to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:12–13). There are two appearings: one past, when grace came in the first coming of Christ, and one future, when glory will come at his return. Christians live between them, and their whole way of life is shaped by both.

The firstfruits

The clearest sign that the age to come has begun is the resurrection of Jesus. The Jews expected the resurrection of the dead at the end of history (Daniel 12:2). What no one expected was that one man would rise first, alone, in the middle of history. Paul explains it with a harvest picture: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

In Israel the firstfruits were the first sheaves of the harvest, brought to God in thanksgiving: not a different crop, but the beginning of the same harvest and the promise of the rest. So Paul says, “Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:23). Easter morning is a piece of the last day placed in the middle of history. The resurrection age has begun in one body, and every believer’s body will follow.

The down payment

The second great sign is the Holy Spirit. The prophets linked the outpouring of the Spirit with the last days, and at Pentecost Peter said that day had come (Acts 2:16–17). Paul says that believers “were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it” (Ephesians 1:13–14).

The word translated “guarantee” was used in business for a first instalment, a deposit that is part of the full price and binds the buyer to pay the rest. The Spirit is not a pledge of something different from himself. He is the first part of the life of the age to come, given now. To have the Spirit is to have heaven’s life already begun in you, and God’s promise that he will finish what he has begun.

Drawing it together

The Reformed scholar Geerhardus Vos drew this as a simple diagram. The line of this age runs on until Christ returns. The line of the age to come begins not at the return but at Christ’s resurrection, and runs above the first until the old line stops. The stretch where the two run together is where we live.

An example

A retired engineer had been a Christian for forty years and found the phrase “the end of the ages” puzzling. Surely, he said, the end was still to come. A younger friend sketched the overlapping lines on a napkin. He looked at it for a long time, then said it explained why his faith had always felt both settled and unfinished. He had thought that tension was a sign of weak faith. Now he saw it was the shape of the age he was living in.

For reflection

Which of these phrases is new to you: “the end of the ages”, “the present evil age”, “the powers of the age to come”? How does calling Christ’s resurrection the “firstfruits” change the way you think about your own future? What would it mean to see the Spirit in you as the first instalment of heaven?

2.title: The World Between the Ages
2.essay:
Look at the world through the lens of the two ages and much that puzzles us begins to make sense. Christ has won, and yet evil is still loud. Both are true, and the New Testament teaches both.

A defeated enemy who still prowls

Jesus said at the cross, “Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). Paul says Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). Satan has been beaten where it matters most: he can no longer hold God’s people under accusation, because their sins have been paid for.

And yet Peter warns, “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Revelation explains why the defeat has made him more frantic, not less: “the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!” (Revelation 12:12). A wounded and cornered enemy is dangerous. But he is not winning, and he cannot win. The same Paul who tells us to stand against his schemes also promises, “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20).

Death defeated, death still at work

Christ partook of flesh and blood “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15). Yet Christians still die and still sit at gravesides. Paul calls death “the last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26). It is the last, which means it is still there, and it is an enemy, which means we are right to hate it. The study Death, Dying & Heaven follows this out.

Hebrews puts the whole tension in two sentences. “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him” (Hebrews 2:8–9). We do not yet see the world put right. We do see Jesus, crowned. Faith looks at him when the world gives no evidence.

A kingdom present but hidden

Jesus’ parables in Matthew 13 were told partly to explain this surprise. Many expected the kingdom to arrive all at once, in plain power. Instead Jesus said it is like a tiny mustard seed that grows into a tree, and like yeast hidden in flour “till it was all leavened” (Matthew 13:33). It begins small and hidden, and it grows.

The parable of the wheat and the weeds speaks most directly to our question. A farmer sows good seed, but an enemy sows weeds among it. The servants want to pull up the weeds at once. The master says, “Let both grow together until the harvest” (Matthew 13:30). Jesus explains that “the field is the world” and “the harvest is the end of the age” (Matthew 13:38–39). God is not careless about evil. He is patient, and his patience gives time for the gospel to be preached. But the sorting will come.

Creation groaning

Paul hears the whole created world in this overlap. “The whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22). Floods, cancers, earthquakes and decay are real evils, not God’s first design. But Paul calls them birth pains. Something is being born. Creation was subjected to frustration “in hope” (Romans 8:20), and it will share in the freedom of God’s children at the resurrection.

The church: an outpost, not yet the capital

Where can the new age be seen now? Above all in the church, a people gathered by the gospel, filled with the Spirit and ruled by Christ’s word. Peter calls believers “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9), and Paul says they “shine as lights in the world” (Philippians 2:15). A local church, meeting in a school hall with worn chairs, is an outpost of the coming city.

But it is an outpost, not yet the capital. Churches still quarrel, still disappoint, still contain hypocrisy and sin. We should neither idolise the church nor despise it. It is the place where the future is breaking in, among people who are not yet what they will be.

Neither triumph nor despair

Two errors lie on either side. Triumphalism forgets the “not yet”. It expects the church to win every cultural battle, every sick person to recover and every revival to sweep the land, and it is shaken or bitter when that does not happen. Despair forgets the “already”. It reads the news and decides that God has lost control, that the gospel no longer works, that we can only hide and wait. The New Testament refuses both. Jesus told his disciples, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Both sentences are his.

An example

A young mother found that the evening news left her anxious and gloomy for hours. War, cruelty and the decline of faith in her country all seemed to say that evil was winning. Her home group read the parable of the wheat and the weeds together. She did not stop caring about the world. But she began to pray differently, for the gospel to grow in hidden places, and to remember that the harvest belongs to the Lord. She also turned the news off earlier.

For reflection

Do you lean more toward triumphalism or toward despair when you look at the world? How does the parable of the wheat and the weeds help you understand God’s patience? What would change if you saw your local church as an outpost of the new age, real but imperfect?

3.title: Already New
3.essay:
Now we bring the pattern home. What is true of the world is true of the believer. If you belong to Christ, the age to come has already begun in you. This unit is about the “already”: what is fully and finally true of you now.

A new creation

Paul says, “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). “New creation” is the language of the prophets for the whole renewed world (Isaiah 65:17). Paul is saying that when someone is joined to Christ, the new creation has begun in that person. You are not merely a better version of your old self. You are a piece of the world to come, living ahead of time.

All this flows from union with Christ, which the study Union with Christ explores at length.

Raised and seated with him

Look at the tenses in Ephesians 2. God, “even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ … and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:5–6). Made alive, raised, seated: all past tense. Paul does not say God will do these things. He says God has done them.

Colossians says the same, and adds the “not yet” in the same breath: “If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Colossians 3:1). “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:3–4). Your life is real, and it is hidden. It is safe with Christ, out of reach of every enemy, but it is not yet on display. One day it will be.

Justified now

The Jews expected God’s verdict on his people at the last judgment. In Christ that verdict has been brought forward. “Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Romans 5:1). “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Notice the word “now”. The verdict of the last day has already been spoken over you, and it is “not guilty”, because Christ bore your sin and his righteousness is counted as yours (2 Corinthians 5:21). It will not be reversed when the books are opened.

This is the bedrock of the Christian life. Your growth is not finished, but your acceptance is. Hebrews puts the two side by side: “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). Perfected, and being sanctified. Both already and not yet, in one verse.

Children now

You are also adopted. “Because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Galatians 4:6). Paul says that son and daughter alike are “no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God” (Galatians 4:7). John marvels at it: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). You do not become God’s child gradually, by getting better. You are his child now, completely, and his love for you will not grow larger when you are more mature.

Indwelt by the Spirit

And the Spirit himself lives in you. “You, however, are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if in fact the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Romans 8:9). Paul then joins this present gift to the future resurrection: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:11). The Spirit who raised Jesus’ body is already at work in yours, and he is the promise that it will be raised too.

What has changed

So what is already, fully and finally true of you, if you trust Christ? You are forgiven for every sin, past, present and future. You are counted righteous. You are God’s adopted child and heir. Your old self, the person you were in Adam, “was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6). Sin is no longer your master. The Spirit lives in you. Your life is hidden with Christ, and nothing can take it from him.

None of this depends on how you feel today. It depends on what God has done in his Son. So you can face your remaining sin honestly without being crushed.

An example

A man in his thirties became a Christian after years of heavy drinking and a broken marriage. When he looked in the mirror he still saw a failure. His pastor asked him to read Ephesians 2:1–10 every morning for a month and to underline every verb that described what God had done. By the end of the month he said something had shifted. He still had a long road ahead, and he knew it. But he had stopped thinking of himself mainly as an ex-drunk. He had started to think of himself as someone God had raised.

For reflection

Which of the “already” truths in this unit do you find hardest to believe about yourself? Why does it matter that the verbs in Ephesians 2:5–6 are in the past tense? How would your day be different if you began it remembering that there is “now no condemnation” for you? What is the difference between becoming God’s child and growing as God’s child?

4.title: Not Yet Finished
4.essay:
If you are already a new creation, why do you still lose your temper, still feel the pull of old sins, still find prayer hard? Because the old age has not yet ended, in the world or in you. The believer is new, and not yet finished.

Flesh and Spirit

Paul writes to Christians, “walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other” (Galatians 5:16–17). By “the flesh” Paul does not mean the body, which God made good, but human nature as shaped by the old age, turned away from God. By “the Spirit” he means the Holy Spirit.

These are not equal forces: the Spirit is God, and the flesh is a defeated power. But the war is real. That inner conflict is the overlap of the ages, running through a single human heart.

Dead to sin, and still fighting it

Romans 6 shows how both can be true. Paul says “our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin” (Romans 6:6). Then he commands: “consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body” (Romans 6:11–12).

To “consider” is not to pretend but to reckon with what is true. Sin is a deposed tyrant still shouting orders, and you are not obliged to obey. “For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14). The study Fighting Sin & Temptation works this out in practical detail.

The cry of Romans 7

Then comes Romans 7:14–25, one of the most honest passages in the Bible. “For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate” (Romans 7:15). “For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind” (Romans 7:22–23). It ends with a groan and a song: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25).

Where Christians differ

Who is the “I” in this passage? Many able interpreters, past and present, read it as a person not yet converted, or as Paul looking back on his life as a Jew under the law, or as anyone trying to keep God’s law in his own strength. They point out that Romans 6 and 8 speak of freedom from sin, and that the man in Romans 7 is “sold under sin” (Romans 7:14), which seems hard to say of a Christian. Some in the holiness tradition go further and see Romans 7 as a stage of the Christian life that can be left behind for a life of steady victory.

This commentary’s view: with Augustine in his later writings, Luther, Calvin and most Reformed teachers, we read Romans 7:14–25 as Paul describing his ongoing life as a believer. He changes to the present tense. He delights in God’s law “in my inner being”, which an unregenerate person does not do. He hates his sin. And he gives thanks for deliverance in Christ while still saying, in the very next sentence, that “with my flesh I serve the law of sin” (Romans 7:25). This is the man of Romans 8, seen from another side. He is a new creation who still lives in the old age, and his groan is the groan of every honest Christian.

Become what you are

Paul’s letters follow a pattern. First he tells you what God has done and who you are (the indicative). Then he tells you what to do (the imperative). The order matters.

One verse shows it plainly. “Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Be clean, because in Christ you are clean. Colossians does the same: you “have put off the old self … and have put on the new self, which is being renewed” (Colossians 3:9–10), so “put to death therefore what is earthly in you” (Colossians 3:5). You do not obey in order to become God’s new creation. You obey because you already are, and you want your life to match the truth.

Without the indicative, the commands become a crushing burden. Without the imperative, the indicative becomes an excuse for laziness. The gospel gives both: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Pressing on, and the day we shall be like him

Paul himself did not claim to have arrived. “Not that I have already obtained this or am already perfect, but I press on to make it my own, because Christ Jesus has made me his own” (Philippians 3:12). The “already” is the reason for the effort, not its reward.

And the struggle will not last for ever. “Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Now, and not yet: in one verse John gives you both. The likeness to Christ that is begun in you now will be finished in an instant when you see him.

An example

A woman who had followed Christ for many years confided to a friend that she still struggled with resentment toward her sister. She felt like a fraud. Her friend opened Romans 7 and 8 and asked whether she delighted in God’s law and hated her bitterness. She said yes, with tears. Her friend said the struggle was evidence that the Spirit was at war in her. She went home and wrote her sister a kind letter, not to prove anything, but because she was already forgiven.

For reflection

Where do you feel the conflict of flesh and Spirit most sharply? Does reading Romans 7 as a Christian’s struggle discourage you or comfort you, and why? Pick one command in Colossians 3 and trace it back to the truth it rests on. How does 1 John 3:2 change the way you face a sin you have fought for years?

5.title: Living in the Overlap
5.essay:
Knowing that we live between the ages is not just theory. It shapes what we expect of ourselves, of God and of this life. Expect too much now and you will be crushed; expect too little and you will give up.

Realistic expectations of change

Christians do change. Paul says “we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). That is real progress. Angry people become gentler. Proud people learn to listen. Addicted people find freedom. But the change is “from one degree … to another”, usually slow, often uneven, sometimes with setbacks. A believer of fifty years still has things to repent of.

This is the normal Christian life, not a failed one. The life is real, and the fruit takes seasons.

Suffering and the inner self

Paul shows how the overlap feels in a body that is ageing and a life that is hard. “So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day. For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:16–17). The outer self belongs to the old age, and it is running down. The inner self belongs to the new age, and it is being renewed. Both are happening in the same person on the same day.

So Paul looks “not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen” (2 Corinthians 4:18). He does not pretend the pain away. He weighs it against glory, and the glory is heavier. The study Christian Suffering treats this more fully.

Healing now and healing then

The overlap of the ages also helps with one of the most painful questions Christians face: why are some people healed in answer to prayer and others not?

God can and does heal now. As a sign of the age to come Jesus “healed all who were sick” (Matthew 8:16), and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray, for “the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up” (James 5:15). Christians should pray for healing, expecting God to hear.

But the New Testament nowhere promises that every illness will be healed in this life. Paul left his co-worker Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Epaphroditus was “ill, near to death” and recovered because “God had mercy on him” (Philippians 2:27), which shows that recovery was a mercy, not a right. Paul pleaded three times for his own “thorn” to be removed, and the answer was, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Christ’s death secures the full healing of his people’s bodies, but the time of that healing is the resurrection. Healings now are tastes of it, given as God wills. So when healing does not come, it is not because the sick person lacked faith. It is because we live in the overlap, where bodies still wear out. And prayer for healing never replaces medical care. Doctors and medicine are among God’s good gifts in a fallen world, and using them is not a failure of faith.

Expecting too much now

Some teaching expects the “already” to be complete. Perfectionist teaching says a Christian can reach a state of no known sin in this life. Prosperity teaching says that health and wealth belong to every believer with enough faith. Some forms of “victorious life” teaching suggest that a second crisis of surrender lifts a Christian above ongoing struggle into steady rest. Those who hold these views want to honour Christ’s power. But they bring the age to come forward too far, and the fruit is often disillusionment, hidden sin, or guilt for illness and poverty that are no one’s fault. The study Perfectionism & Self-Condemnation deals with the inner version of this error.

Expecting too little

Others give up on the “already”. They say, “I will never change. This is just who I am.” That forgets that the Spirit of the resurrection lives in them. Defeatism can feel like humility, but it doubts God’s power.

Sometimes, though, what feels like defeat is something more. When a struggle has become depression, anxiety or an addiction, a Christian should talk to a pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask for a medical check-up. If the doctor recommends treatment, receiving it is not a lack of faith. And if you ever find yourself thinking about ending your life, tell someone at once: call emergency services or a crisis line, or speak to a trusted person today.

Assurance when sin remains

How can you be sure you belong to Christ when you still sin? Not by finding a clean record. John writes so that we may not sin, “but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). Assurance rests first on Christ and his promises. Then it is confirmed by signs of the Spirit’s life: you trust Christ, you hate your sin, you return to him when you fall, and you love his people. The fight itself is one of those signs. The old age remains in you, but so does the Saviour who holds you, and “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

An example

A man with chronic pain had been told at a conference that if he truly believed he would be healed. Months later he was no better and felt that God was disappointed in him. His minister read 2 Corinthians 12 with him, prayed with him for healing, and urged him to keep seeing his consultant. The pain stayed. But the guilt lifted. He began to see his weakness as a place where Christ’s strength could rest, while he waited for the day his body will be made new.

For reflection

Are you more tempted to expect too much now or too little? How does 2 Corinthians 4:16–18 help you see your own ageing or suffering? What would you say to a friend who thinks illness means a lack of faith? On what do you rest your assurance when sin remains?

6.title: When Not Yet Becomes Now
6.essay:
The overlap will not last for ever. One day the night will end, and the day that has been dawning will fully come. The Christian life is shaped by that day, and is lived toward it.

The return of the King

The New Testament looks ahead to one great event: the return of Jesus Christ in glory. “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). The Jesus who rose as the firstfruits will come to bring in the harvest.

Christians differ over the order of events around that day. Premillennialists expect a thousand-year reign of Christ on earth after his return. Postmillennialists expect the gospel to bring a long age of blessing before it. This commentary’s view is amillennial: Christ reigns now, the “thousand years” of Revelation 20 is the present age, and there will be one return of Christ, followed by the resurrection of all, the last judgment and the new creation. The study End Times Models sets out the views fairly. All agree on the main thing: he is coming.

The body raised

On that day the overlap of the ages ends in the body of every believer. “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet” (1 Corinthians 15:51–52). The body that was “sown in weakness” is “raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:43). Christ “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21).

Notice what is raised. Not a ghost, not a new person, but you, in a body made new. The Spirit who lives in you now, as the first instalment, will finish his work. And in that instant the war within will be over. The flesh that has fought the Spirit all your Christian life will be gone. “We shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). Then Paul’s taunt will come true: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

All things new

And the world will be made new too. John saw “a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away” (Revelation 21:1). The groaning creation will be set free. God himself will live with his people. “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). Then the One on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

He says “making”, not “will make”. The work has already begun, in the risen Christ, in the Spirit, in every new heart. The last day does not start the new creation. It completes it. What dawned at the empty tomb will fill the whole sky. There will be no more overlap, only the age to come, with no shadow left in it. And at the centre of it all will be the Lamb who was slain, whose cross and empty tomb made it possible. Every tear wiped away will have been paid for by his.

People of the future, living now

So how should we live while we wait? Titus 2 answers. The grace that has appeared trains us to live godly lives “in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope” (Titus 2:12–13). Christ “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14). And John says, “everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure” (1 John 3:3). Hope is not idle. Christians practise now the life of the age that is coming.

How to pray

Pray both ways. Pray with confidence, because the age to come is already here and the King hears. Ask for real change, real healing, real conversions, real growth in holiness. And pray with longing, because it is not yet fully here. The Lord’s Prayer does both: “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). The Bible’s last prayer is the cry of the overlap: “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

How to fight

Fight sin as someone who has already won. You are not fighting to become God’s child. You are fighting because you are. “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13). Expect a long war, but not a lost one. When you fall, get up at once and go back to Christ, your advocate.

How to wait and hope

Wait with patience. “If we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Romans 8:25). Patience is faithful work done in the meantime, because “in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Every act of love, every prayer, every small obedience is building with materials that will last into the new creation.

And hope with certainty. Christian hope is not wishful thinking. It rests on a resurrection that has already happened and a Spirit who is already given. The firstfruits are in. The deposit has been paid. The sky is already light in the east.

An example

An elderly widower with failing eyesight spent his evenings listening to Revelation 21 and 22 read aloud. A neighbour asked whether it made him sad, thinking of all he had lost. He said it did the opposite. He had seen the morning begin in his own life when he came to Christ sixty years before, and he had watched it grow, slowly, through many hard nights. Now, he said, he was simply waiting for full daylight.

For reflection

How does knowing that the struggle with sin will one day end help you to keep fighting today? What does it mean that God speaks of making all things new in the present tense? Which of the four, praying, fighting, waiting or hoping, do you most need to grow in? How might you live this week as someone who belongs to the age to come?
